levels.name: The Three-Sided Path
levels.storyContext: Sage Multiplico explains that all paths in the mountains have shapes with meaning.

problems.statement: "Welcome, young explorer! This path is made of triangles. Count the sides of this shape. How many sides does a triangle have?"

hints.text: What does "side" mean for a shape? Think about the straight edges.
Count each straight edge of the triangle one by one.
Start at one corner and trace around — how many edges do you pass?

problems.solutionExplanation: 3 — a triangle has exactly 3 straight sides, one connecting each pair of corners.
problems.teachingPoint: A triangle always has exactly 3 sides and 3 vertices.

problems.statement: "Which of these is NOT a triangle? A) A shape with 3 straight sides B) A shape with 3 angles C) A shape with 4 corners D) A shape with 3 vertices"

hints.text: A triangle has exactly 3 sides, 3 angles, and 3 vertices.
If a shape has 4 corners, how many sides must it have?
4 corners = 4 sides = quadrilateral, not a triangle.

problems.solutionExplanation: C — a shape with 4 corners has 4 sides and is a quadrilateral, not a triangle.
problems.teachingPoint: A triangle always has exactly 3 sides, 3 angles, and 3 vertices. More or fewer means it is not a triangle.

problems.statement: "A triangle has one 90-degree angle. What is this type of triangle called? A) Equilateral B) Right C) Obtuse D) Acute"

hints.text: A 90-degree angle is called a right angle. What triangle has a right angle?
The type of triangle is named after its most notable angle feature.
A triangle with a 90-degree angle is a right triangle.

problems.solutionExplanation: A right triangle has exactly one 90-degree angle (a right angle).
problems.teachingPoint: Right triangles have one 90° angle. They are special because they connect to the Pythagorean theorem.

levels.name: Classifying Triangles
levels.storyContext: The mountain wall displays three triangles carved by ancient mathematicians.

problems.statement: "Look at these three triangles on the mountain wall. Which one has all sides the same length?" Triangle A: sides 5, 5, 5 Triangle B: sides 5, 5, 3 Triangle C: sides 3, 4, 5

hints.text: What does "all sides the same length" mean mathematically?
Compare the three numbers listed for each triangle — which set has all identical values?
Check Triangle A: are 5, 5, and 5 all the same number?

problems.solutionExplanation: Triangle A (sides 5, 5, 5) — all three sides are equal, making it equilateral.
problems.teachingPoint: Equilateral means all sides equal, isosceles means exactly two sides equal, scalene means no sides equal.

problems.statement: "A triangle has sides of length 4, 4, and 4. Is it equilateral, isosceles, or scalene?"

hints.text: How many sides are equal in this triangle?
All three sides are 4. A triangle with all equal sides has a special name.
All sides equal = equilateral. (It is also isosceles, since at least 2 sides match.)

problems.solutionExplanation: Equilateral — all three sides are equal (4, 4, 4). An equilateral triangle is a special isosceles triangle.
problems.teachingPoint: Equilateral = 3 equal sides. Isosceles = at least 2 equal sides. Scalene = no equal sides.

problems.statement: "Is a 120-degree angle acute, right, or obtuse? A) Acute B) Right C) Obtuse"

hints.text: Angles are classified by their size relative to 90 degrees.
Acute < 90°. Right = 90°. Obtuse > 90°. Where does 120° fall?
120° > 90°, so it is obtuse.

problems.solutionExplanation: Obtuse — 120° is greater than 90°. Acute angles are less than 90°, right angles are exactly 90°.
problems.teachingPoint: Angle classification: acute (< 90°), right (= 90°), obtuse (> 90° and < 180°).

levels.name: Triangle Side Challenge
levels.storyContext: A bridge shaped like a triangle stretches across a ravine.

problems.statement: "The mountain bridge has an isosceles triangle shape. Two sides are 9 units and one side is 4 units. What are all the side lengths?"

hints.text: What does "isosceles" mean about the sides?
An isosceles triangle has exactly two sides that are equal in length.
You know two sides are 9 and one is 4 — list all three: the two equal ones and the different one.

problems.teachingPoint: An isosceles triangle has exactly two equal sides — knowing this lets you find all three side lengths from just two values.

problems.statement: "An equilateral triangle has perimeter 27 cm. What is the length of one side?"

hints.text: All sides of an equilateral triangle are equal.
If 3 equal sides sum to 27, each side is 27 ÷ 3.

problems.solutionExplanation: 9 cm — an equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides, so 27 ÷ 3 = 9.
problems.teachingPoint: Equilateral triangle: perimeter = 3 × side, so side = perimeter ÷ 3.

problems.statement: "A triangle has angles of 60°, 60°, and 60°. What type is it? A) Acute B) Right C) Obtuse D) Cannot exist"

hints.text: Check each angle: are any ≥ 90°?
All three angles are 60°, which is less than 90°.
Since all angles are acute (< 90°), this is an acute triangle. It is also equilateral!

problems.solutionExplanation: Acute — all three angles (60°) are less than 90°. This is also an equilateral triangle.
problems.teachingPoint: An acute triangle has ALL angles less than 90°. An equilateral triangle is always acute.

problems.statement: "Can a triangle have two right angles (two 90° angles)? Explain why or why not."

correctAnswer.value: No. Two right angles = 180°, leaving 0° for the third angle, which is impossible.
correctAnswer.displayValue: No — angles would sum to more than 180°

hints.text: The angles in any triangle must add up to exactly 180°.
If two angles are 90° each, that is already 180°. What would the third angle be?
The third angle would be 0°, which means no triangle. So two right angles is impossible.

problems.solutionExplanation: No — two 90° angles sum to 180°, leaving 0° for the third angle. A triangle needs positive angles summing to 180°.
problems.teachingPoint: Triangle angle sum = 180°. At most ONE angle can be right or obtuse.

levels.name: The Quadrilateral Crossing
levels.storyContext: The path crosses a bridge shaped like a four-sided figure.

problems.statement: "This bridge has 4 sides. What do we call a shape with 4 sides?"

hints.text: The prefix "quad" gives a clue about the number of sides.
"Quad" means 4 in Latin — what shape name uses this prefix?
The word starts with "Quad" and ends with "lateral" (meaning sides).

problems.solutionExplanation: Quadrilateral — "quad" means 4 and "lateral" means sides.
problems.teachingPoint: "Quad" means 4, "lateral" refers to sides.

problems.statement: "A quadrilateral has how many angles?"

hints.text: A quadrilateral has 4 sides. How many corners (angles) does it have?
Each side meets another at a corner. 4 sides = 4 corners.
4 angles. The number of sides equals the number of angles in any polygon.

problems.solutionExplanation: 4 — a quadrilateral has 4 sides, 4 vertices, and 4 angles.
problems.teachingPoint: In any polygon, the number of sides = number of angles = number of vertices.

problems.statement: "Which shape has 4 equal sides but does NOT have to have right angles? A) Square B) Rhombus C) Rectangle D) Trapezoid"

hints.text: Think about which quadrilaterals have all 4 sides equal.
A square has 4 equal sides AND right angles. A rhombus has 4 equal sides but angles can vary.
A rhombus is like a tilted square — 4 equal sides, but angles need not be 90°.

problems.solutionExplanation: Rhombus — it has 4 equal sides but its angles need not be right angles. A square is a special rhombus WITH right angles.
problems.teachingPoint: A rhombus has 4 equal sides. A square is a rhombus with right angles. Every square is a rhombus, but not every rhombus is a square.

levels.name: Special Quadrilaterals
levels.storyContext: The mountain path is paved with four-sided stone tiles.

problems.statement: "Match each quadrilateral to its description: A. Square B. Rectangle C. Parallelogram Which one has 4 equal sides AND 4 right angles?"

hints.text: What properties does a square have that other quadrilaterals might not?
A square has TWO special properties: equal sides AND right angles. Which option matches both?
Check option A (Square) — does it have 4 equal sides AND 4 right angles?

problems.solutionExplanation: A (Square) — it is the only quadrilateral with both 4 equal sides and 4 right angles.
problems.teachingPoint: A square is special because it is BOTH a rectangle (4 right angles) and a rhombus (4 equal sides).

problems.statement: "Lines that go in the same direction and never meet are called: A) Perpendicular B) Parallel C) Intersecting D) Adjacent"

hints.text: Think about railroad tracks — they run side by side and never cross.
Lines that never meet, no matter how far extended, are called what?
Parallel lines never intersect. Perpendicular lines meet at right angles.

problems.solutionExplanation: Parallel — lines that never meet. Like railroad tracks extending forever without touching.
problems.teachingPoint: Parallel lines never meet. Perpendicular lines meet at 90°. Knowing the difference is essential for geometry.

problems.statement: "Two lines meet at a 90° angle. They are: A) Parallel B) Perpendicular C) Curved D) Skew"

hints.text: Lines that meet at right angles have a special name.
A 90° angle is a right angle. Lines forming a right angle are called...
Perpendicular lines meet at exactly 90°.

problems.solutionExplanation: Perpendicular — two lines forming a 90° angle. The corner of a book shows perpendicular edges.
problems.teachingPoint: Perpendicular lines form 90° angles. They create the corners of rectangles and squares.

problems.statement: "A rectangle has two pairs of parallel sides. Does a trapezoid have two pairs of parallel sides? How many?"

correctAnswer.value: No, a trapezoid has exactly one pair of parallel sides.

hints.text: Compare: rectangle has 2 pairs of parallel sides. How many does a trapezoid have?
In a trapezoid, one pair of sides is parallel and the other pair is not.
Exactly one pair of parallel sides defines a trapezoid.

problems.solutionExplanation: A trapezoid has exactly one pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram (like a rectangle) has two pairs.
problems.teachingPoint: Trapezoid = exactly 1 pair of parallel sides. Parallelogram = 2 pairs. This is a key classification difference.

levels.name: Polygon Peaks
levels.storyContext: Polygon Peaks

problems.statement: "The summit marker is a shape with 5 sides. What is this polygon called?"

hints.text: Polygon names come from Greek number prefixes. What prefix means 5?
"Penta" means 5 in Greek — what shape name starts with "penta"?
The word is "Penta" + "gon" (meaning angles/corners).

problems.solutionExplanation: Pentagon — "penta" means 5, and a pentagon has 5 sides and 5 angles.
problems.teachingPoint: Pentagon (5), Hexagon (6), Heptagon (7), Octagon (8)

problems.statement: "How many sides does an octagon have?"

hints.text: Oct- means 8 in Latin/Greek (like octopus has 8 arms).
Count: tri=3, quad=4, pent=5, hex=6, hept=7, oct=?
Octagon = 8 sides.

problems.solutionExplanation: 8 — "oct" means 8 (octopus = 8 arms, octagon = 8 sides).
problems.teachingPoint: Polygon prefixes: tri=3, quad=4, pent=5, hex=6, hept=7, oct=8.

problems.statement: "A stop sign is what shape? A) Hexagon B) Pentagon C) Octagon D) Heptagon"

hints.text: Picture a stop sign in your mind. How many sides does it have?
Count the sides of a stop sign: it has 8 equal sides.
A regular octagon. Stop signs are the most famous real-world octagon.

problems.solutionExplanation: Octagon — a stop sign has 8 sides, making it a regular octagon.
problems.teachingPoint: Recognizing shapes in the real world builds geometry intuition. Stop sign = octagon is a classic example.

levels.name: Count the Sides
levels.storyContext: Summit markers come in many shapes — count their sides to identify them.

problems.statement: "How many sides does a hexagon have? And an octagon?"

hints.text: Like "pentagon" uses "penta" for 5, what prefixes mean 6 and 8?
"Hex" means 6 and "Oct" means 8 — these are Greek number prefixes.
Hexagon = hex (6) + gon. How many sides? Now do the same for octagon.

problems.solutionExplanation: Hexagon = 6 sides, Octagon = 8 sides. The Greek prefixes "hex" and "oct" tell you the count.
problems.teachingPoint: Greek prefixes tell you the number of sides: penta=5, hexa=6, hepta=7, octa=8.

problems.statement: "A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal. Is a rectangle always a regular polygon?"

correctAnswer.value: No. A rectangle has equal angles (all 90°) but not always equal sides. Only a square is a regular quadrilateral.
correctAnswer.displayValue: No — only a square is regular

hints.text: For a polygon to be regular, it needs equal sides AND equal angles.
A rectangle has all angles equal (90°). But are all sides equal?
Only if length = width, which makes it a square. So only squares are regular quadrilaterals.

problems.solutionExplanation: No — a rectangle has equal angles but not necessarily equal sides. Only a square is both, making it a regular quadrilateral.
problems.teachingPoint: Regular polygon = equal sides AND equal angles. A square is the only regular quadrilateral.

problems.statement: "Order these polygons by number of sides (fewest to most): Hexagon, Triangle, Pentagon, Quadrilateral"

hints.text: Recall the number of sides each polygon has.
Triangle=3, Quadrilateral=4, Pentagon=5, Hexagon=6.
Order: 3, 4, 5, 6 = Triangle, Quadrilateral, Pentagon, Hexagon.

problems.solutionExplanation: Triangle (3), Quadrilateral (4), Pentagon (5), Hexagon (6).
problems.teachingPoint: Polygon side counts: tri=3, quad=4, pent=5, hex=6, hept=7, oct=8.

levels.name: Polyomino Puzzle
levels.storyContext: Crystal fragments in the cave are shaped like connected squares.

problems.statement: "A tetromino is made of 4 unit squares. How many unit squares make up a pentomino?"

hints.text: Notice how the name changes with the number: domino (2), tromino (3), tetromino (4)...
The prefix tells you the count. "Pent" means 5 — like pentagon.
If a tetromino has 4 squares and uses "tetra" (4), a pentomino uses "penta" (5), so...

problems.solutionExplanation: 5 — polyomino names use Greek number prefixes: "penta" means 5, so a pentomino has 5 unit squares.
problems.teachingPoint: Polyominoes are named by their number of squares (domino = 2, tromino = 3, tetromino = 4, pentomino = 5).

problems.statement: "How many different tetrominoes (shapes made of 4 squares) exist? A) 3 B) 5 C) 7 D) 12"

hints.text: Try building all possible shapes with 4 connected squares.
You can make: I (line), O (square), T, S, L shapes.
There are exactly 5 distinct tetrominoes (not counting rotations/reflections).

problems.solutionExplanation: 5 — the I, O, T, S, and L tetrominoes. These are the same pieces used in Tetris!
problems.teachingPoint: Systematic enumeration: list all possibilities, eliminate duplicates (rotations/reflections count as same shape).

levels.name: Build the Shape
levels.storyContext: Crystal fragments must be arranged to fill the cave floor.

problems.statement: "Using exactly 5 unit squares connected edge-to-edge, draw a pentomino that fits inside a 3×3 grid. How many different pentominoes can you make?"

correctAnswer.value: There are 12 distinct pentominoes (not counting rotations/reflections as different). Students need to draw any valid pentomino.
correctAnswer.displayValue: There are 12 distinct pentominoes (not counting rotations/reflections as different). Students need to draw any valid pentomino.

hints.text: Start by thinking about what shapes you can make with 5 connected squares.
Try building pentominoes systematically — start with a row of 5, then try L-shapes, T-shapes, etc.
There are more than 10 but fewer than 15. Try drawing all the ones that fit in a 3×3 grid first.

problems.solutionExplanation: There are 12 distinct pentominoes when rotations and reflections are not counted as different shapes.
problems.teachingPoint: There are exactly 12 distinct pentominoes — systematic counting prevents missing any or counting duplicates.

problems.statement: "How many pentominoes (shapes made of 5 connected squares) exist? Count rotations and reflections as the same shape."

hints.text: This is harder than tetrominoes. Try building them systematically.
Start with the I-pentomino (line of 5). Then add squares in different positions.
There are exactly 12 distinct pentominoes. They are often named with letters: F, I, L, N, P, T, U, V, W, X, Y, Z.

problems.solutionExplanation: 12 — there are exactly 12 pentominoes (often labeled F, I, L, N, P, T, U, V, W, X, Y, Z).
problems.teachingPoint: Systematic counting is a key math skill — enumerate all cases, then remove duplicates.

problems.statement: "Each pentomino covers 5 unit squares. If you could use ALL 12 pentominoes once, how many total unit squares would they cover?"

hints.text: If each pentomino covers 5 squares, and there are 12 pentominoes...
Total = 12 × 5 = ?
12 × 5 = 60 squares. This means they could tile a 6×10 or 5×12 rectangle!

problems.solutionExplanation: 60 — 12 pentominoes × 5 squares each = 60 total squares.
problems.teachingPoint: 12 pentominoes × 5 squares = 60 total squares. This is why they can tile 6×10, 5×12, 4×15, and 3×20 rectangles.

levels.name: Polyomino Tiling Challenge
levels.storyContext: The ancient cave has a rectangular floor made entirely of pentominoes...

problems.statement: "Can you tile a 5×4 rectangle using exactly 4 pentominoes (with no overlaps and no gaps)? How many unit squares does the rectangle have, and does 4 pentominoes provide enough?"

correctAnswer.displayValue: 20 square units, and yes, 4 pentominoes × 5 squares = 20

hints.text: First calculate the area of the rectangle: 5 × 4 = ?
Each pentomino covers exactly 5 unit squares. How many squares do 4 pentominoes cover?
4 × 5 = 20 = 5 × 4. The areas match! So a tiling is possible (and many solutions exist).

problems.solutionExplanation: 20 square units. 4 pentominoes × 5 squares each = 20, which exactly covers the 5×4 = 20 rectangle. Multiple valid tilings exist.
problems.teachingPoint: Area conservation: a tiling is only possible if the total piece area equals the rectangle area. This is necessary but not always sufficient.

problems.statement: "Can ALL 12 pentominoes tile a 6 × 10 rectangle with no gaps or overlaps? A) Yes B) No C) Impossible to know"

hints.text: 12 pentominoes × 5 squares = 60 squares. Does 6 × 10 = 60?
The area matches (60 = 60). But can the shapes actually fit? This is a famous puzzle.
Yes! There are over 2,000 different solutions for tiling a 6×10 rectangle with all 12 pentominoes.

problems.solutionExplanation: Yes! There are 2,339 ways to tile a 6×10 rectangle with all 12 pentominoes.
problems.teachingPoint: Area matching is necessary but not sufficient for tiling. For pentominoes in a 6×10, it works — this is a classic combinatorics result.

levels.name: Shapes & Angles Quiz
levels.storyContext: Test your shape knowledge before the next trail!

problems.statement: "How many sides does a hexagon have? A) 5 B) 6 C) 7 D) 8"

hints.text: Hex- means 6 (like hexadecimal = base 16).
Pent=5, Hex=6, Hept=7, Oct=8.
Hexagon = 6 sides.

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 — hexagon means 6-sided polygon.
problems.teachingPoint: Hex = 6. Hexagon = 6-sided polygon.

problems.statement: "A triangle has sides 5, 5, and 3. It is: A) Equilateral B) Isosceles C) Scalene D) Right"

hints.text: Count how many sides are equal.
Two sides are 5, one is 3. Exactly 2 equal sides = ?
Isosceles means at least 2 equal sides. Here, exactly 2 are equal.

problems.solutionExplanation: Isosceles — two sides are equal (5, 5) and one is different (3).
problems.teachingPoint: Isosceles = at least 2 equal sides. Equilateral = all 3 equal. Scalene = none equal.

problems.statement: "What type of angle is 45°? A) Acute B) Right C) Obtuse D) Straight"

hints.text: Compare 45° to the right angle benchmark of 90°.
45° < 90°. Angles less than 90° are called...
Acute! Acute angles are less than 90°.

problems.solutionExplanation: Acute — 45° is less than 90°.
problems.teachingPoint: Acute < 90°, Right = 90°, Obtuse = 90° to 180°, Straight = 180°.

problems.statement: "Name a quadrilateral that has 4 equal sides. Name one with 4 right angles. Name one with both."

correctAnswer.displayValue: Rhombus (4 equal sides), Rectangle (4 right angles), Square (both)

hints.text: Think about the special quadrilateral family.
4 equal sides: rhombus. 4 right angles: rectangle. Both: ?
A square has 4 equal sides AND 4 right angles. It is both a rhombus and a rectangle.

problems.solutionExplanation: Rhombus (4 equal sides), Rectangle (4 right angles), Square (both). A square is a special rhombus AND a special rectangle.
problems.teachingPoint: The quadrilateral hierarchy: square ⊂ rhombus, square ⊂ rectangle, both ⊂ parallelogram.

problems.statement: "Grogg says a rhombus is always a square because both have 4 equal sides. Find his error."

correctAnswer.value: A square needs 4 equal sides AND 4 right angles. A rhombus has 4 equal sides but not necessarily right angles.
correctAnswer.displayValue: A rhombus needs right angles to be a square.

hints.text: What does a square require that a rhombus does not?
A square has 4 equal sides AND 4 right angles. A rhombus only requires 4 equal sides.
A tilted rhombus has no right angles, so it is not a square. Every square IS a rhombus, but not vice versa.

problems.solutionExplanation: A rhombus only needs 4 equal sides. A square also needs 4 right angles. So not every rhombus is a square.
problems.teachingPoint: The relationship: every square is a rhombus, but not every rhombus is a square. The extra requirement is right angles.

levels.name: Counting by 2s
levels.storyContext: The cave crystals glow in a rhythmic pattern as you walk.

problems.statement: "The cave crystals glow every 2 steps. Starting at 2, what are the next 5 numbers you'll see glowing crystals?"

hints.text: Skip-counting means adding the same number over and over.
Start at 2, then add 2 each time: 2, 2+2=?, 4+2=?, ...
Write out: 2, 4, ... now add 2 three more times.

problems.solutionExplanation: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 — each number is 2 more than the previous one (repeated addition of 2).
problems.teachingPoint: Skip-counting is repeated addition: 2, 2+2, 2+2+2...

problems.statement: "Count by 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8, ___, 12. What number fills the blank?"

hints.text: You are counting by 2s. Each number is 2 more than the last.
After 8, add 2 more.

problems.solutionExplanation: 10 — counting by 2s: 8 + 2 = 10.
problems.teachingPoint: Skip-counting by 2s: add 2 each time.

problems.statement: "When counting by 2s starting from 0, will you ever say the number 15? A) Yes B) No"

hints.text: All numbers when counting by 2 from 0 are even.
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. Does 15 end in one of these?
15 ends in 5, so it is odd and will never appear in skip-counting by 2.

problems.solutionExplanation: No — counting by 2 from 0 produces only even numbers, and 15 is odd.
problems.teachingPoint: Skip-counting by 2 from 0 produces all even numbers. Odd numbers are never reached.

levels.name: Counting by 5s
levels.storyContext: Stepping stones mark every 5th pace through the cavern.

problems.statement: "Count by 5s from 5 to 50. Circle all the numbers that end in 0."

hints.text: First list all numbers when counting by 5s from 5 to 50.
The count goes 5, 10, 15, 20... Which of these end in the digit 0?
Look at the ones place of each number. Circle only those where the ones digit is 0.

problems.teachingPoint: When skip-counting by 5, numbers alternate between ending in 5 and ending in 0.

problems.statement: "Count by 5s: 5, 10, 15, ___, 25. What is missing?"

hints.text: Each step adds 5.

problems.solutionExplanation: 20 — counting by 5s: 15 + 5 = 20.
problems.teachingPoint: Skip-counting by 5: numbers always end in 0 or 5.

problems.statement: "If you count by 5s starting from 5, what is the 8th number? A) 35 B) 40 C) 45 D) 50"

hints.text: The nth number in skip-counting by 5 is 5 × n.
Getting closer: 5 × 8 = ?
5 × 8 = 40. The 8th number is 40.

problems.solutionExplanation: 40 — the 8th multiple of 5 is 5 × 8 = 40.
problems.teachingPoint: Skip-counting connects to multiplication: the nth number when counting by k is k × n.

levels.name: Counting by Different Numbers
levels.storyContext: Stalactites drip at regular intervals, each marking a count.

problems.statement: "Skip-count by 4s starting at 4. What is the 7th number in your count?"

hints.text: The 7th number means you add 4 a total of 7 times starting from 0, or count 7 groups of 4.
Write out the sequence: 4, 8, 12, 16, ... Keep going until you reach the 7th number.
You have 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24... what comes next?

problems.solutionExplanation: 28 — the sequence is 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28. The 7th number is 7 × 4 = 28.
problems.teachingPoint: The nth number when skip-counting by k is just n × k — skip-counting IS multiplication.

problems.statement: "Count by 3s: 3, 6, 9, ___, 15. What fills the blank?"

hints.text: Add 3 each time.
Getting closer: 9 + 3 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 12 — counting by 3s: 9 + 3 = 12.
problems.teachingPoint: Skip-counting by 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15... These are the multiples of 3.

problems.statement: "You count by 4s starting from 4. Which number will you NOT say? A) 16 B) 20 C) 22 D) 24"

hints.text: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24... Is 22 in this list?
20 + 4 = 24. 22 is between 20 and 24.
22 is not a multiple of 4. You would skip from 20 to 24.

problems.solutionExplanation: 22 — it is not a multiple of 4. The sequence goes 20, 24 (skipping 22).
problems.teachingPoint: Skip-counting by n only hits multiples of n. Numbers in between are skipped.

levels.name: The Hundreds Chart
levels.storyContext: The cave wall shows an ancient hundreds chart.

problems.statement: "On the hundreds chart, start at 7. Add 10. Where do you land? Add 10 again. What pattern do you notice?"

value: 7 → 17 → 27. Pattern: The ones digit stays the same
correctAnswer.displayValue: 7 → 17 → 27. Pattern: The ones digit stays the same, the tens digit increases by 1.

hints.text: Adding 10 moves you down one row on the hundreds chart. What stays the same?
Try it: 7, then 7+10=17, then 17+10=27. Look at the ones digit each time.
The ones digit stays at 7 each time. What happens to the tens digit?

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 → 17 → 27. The pattern: the ones digit stays the same (7), the tens digit increases by 1 each time.
problems.teachingPoint: Adding 10 on a hundreds chart moves down one row — the ones digit never changes, only the tens digit increases by 1.

problems.statement: "On a hundreds chart, the multiples of 5 form a pattern. What is it? A) Diagonal line B) Two vertical columns C) Horizontal rows D) Scattered"

hints.text: Multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5. Where do those appear on a hundreds chart?
Numbers ending in 5 are in one column, numbers ending in 0 in another.
Two vertical columns: the 5s column and the 10s column.

problems.solutionExplanation: Two vertical columns — multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5, forming two columns on the hundreds chart.
problems.teachingPoint: Patterns on the hundreds chart reveal multiplication structure visually.

levels.name: Chart Patterns
levels.storyContext: The cave wall displays an ancient hundreds chart carved in stone.

problems.statement: "What do all numbers in this sequence have in common: 3, 13, 23, 33, 43?"

correctAnswer.value: They all have 3 in the ones place.
correctAnswer.displayValue: They all have 3 in the ones place.

hints.text: Look at each number carefully. What digit appears in every number?
Check the ones place: 3, 13, 23, 33, 43. What digit is always there?
Every number ends in 3 — they all share the same ones digit.

problems.solutionExplanation: They all have 3 in the ones place — they form a column on the hundreds chart.
problems.teachingPoint: Numbers in the same column of a hundreds chart always share the same ones digit.

problems.statement: "What pattern do multiples of 9 follow in their digits? (Hint: look at 9, 18, 27, 36, 45...)"

correctAnswer.value: The digits always add up to 9

hints.text: Add the digits of each: 9→9, 18→1+8=9, 27→2+7=9...
Every multiple of 9 has digits that sum to 9 (or a multiple of 9).
The digit-sum rule: a number is divisible by 9 if its digits sum to 9.

problems.solutionExplanation: The digits of every multiple of 9 add up to 9: 9, 18(1+8=9), 27(2+7=9), 36(3+6=9)...
problems.teachingPoint: The digit-sum rule for 9 is a powerful shortcut for checking divisibility.

problems.statement: "Is 132 a multiple of 3? Use the digit-sum test. A) Yes B) No"

hints.text: Add the digits of 132.
1 + 3 + 2 = 6. Is 6 divisible by 3?
Yes! 6 ÷ 3 = 2. So 132 is a multiple of 3.

problems.solutionExplanation: Yes — digit sum = 1+3+2 = 6, and 6 is divisible by 3.
problems.teachingPoint: Divisibility by 3: if the digit sum is divisible by 3, the number is too.

levels.name: Skip-Count Intersection
levels.storyContext: Two rivers of glowing crystals intersect deep in the cave.

problems.statement: "Ben skip-counts by 6s starting at 6. Jen skip-counts by 9s starting at 9. What is the largest two-digit number that Ben and Jen both say?"

hints.text: What numbers appear in BOTH skip-count sequences? These are common multiples.
List multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24... and multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36... Find overlaps.
Common multiples of 6 and 9 are: 18, 36, 54, 72, 90. Which is the largest two-digit number?

problems.solutionExplanation: Multiples of both 6 and 9: 18, 36, 54, 72, 90. The largest two-digit one is 90.
problems.teachingPoint: Common multiples appear in both skip-count sequences — the smallest common multiple of 6 and 9 is 18 (their LCM).

problems.statement: "What is the smallest number that appears in BOTH the skip-count-by-3 and skip-count-by-4 sequences? (Starting from 0)"

hints.text: List multiples of 3: 3,6,9,12... and multiples of 4: 4,8,12...
Look for the first number in both lists.
The first common number is 12 (= 3×4).

problems.solutionExplanation: 12 — the LCM of 3 and 4. Multiples of 3: 3,6,9,12. Multiples of 4: 4,8,12. First overlap: 12.
problems.teachingPoint: The least common multiple (LCM) is the smallest number in both skip-count sequences.

levels.name: Balance Scale Introduction
levels.storyContext: An old balance scale sits at the cave entrance.

problems.statement: "A balance scale has 15 on the left side. What must go on the right side to balance?"

hints.text: What does "balance" mean? Think about what makes a seesaw level.
A balanced scale means both sides weigh the same amount.
If the left side shows 15, what number on the right makes them equal?

problems.solutionExplanation: 15 — a balanced scale means both sides are equal, so the right side must also be 15.
problems.teachingPoint: When a scale balances, both sides are equal.

problems.statement: "A balance has 15 on the left side. The right side has 7 + ___. What goes in the blank?"

hints.text: Both sides must be equal.

problems.solutionExplanation: 8 — because 7 + 8 = 15, balancing both sides.
problems.teachingPoint: A balance scale shows equality: left side = right side. Find the missing number by subtraction.

levels.name: Missing Number Balance
levels.storyContext: The balance scale holds weights on both sides.

problems.statement: "The left side has: 20 + 10. The right side has: 15 + ___. What goes in the blank to balance?"

hints.text: First figure out what the left side totals. Then the right side must match.
Left side: 20 + 10 = 30. So the right side must also equal 30.
Right side is 15 + ___. What plus 15 equals 30?

problems.solutionExplanation: 15 — the left side totals 30 (20+10), so the right side needs 15+15=30 to balance.
problems.teachingPoint: Balance problems are equations in disguise — both sides must be equal, so find the missing value.

problems.statement: "If 3 × □ = 24, what is □?"

hints.text: This is a missing-factor problem.

problems.solutionExplanation: 8 — because 3 × 8 = 24.
problems.teachingPoint: Missing factor = divide: if a × □ = c, then □ = c ÷ a.

hints.text: Three identical values sum to 21.

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 — because 3 × 7 = 21.
problems.teachingPoint: Repeated addition of the same number IS multiplication: □ + □ + □ = 3 × □.

levels.name: Multi-Step Balance
levels.storyContext: The ultimate balance challenge guards the cave exit.

problems.statement: "If 3 triangles balance with 12, how many triangles balance with 20?"

hints.text: First find what ONE triangle is worth using the first balance.
If 3 triangles = 12, divide to find one triangle: 12 ÷ 3 = ?
Each triangle equals 4. Now how many 4s make 20?

problems.solutionExplanation: 5 — each triangle weighs 4 (12 ÷ 3 = 4), so 20 ÷ 4 = 5 triangles balance with 20.
problems.teachingPoint: Solving balance problems step-by-step: first find the unit value, then scale to the target.

hints.text: Work backwards: undo the +3 first.

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 — undo step by step: 17-3=14, 14÷2=7.
problems.teachingPoint: Multi-step equations: undo operations in reverse order (PEMDAS backwards).

levels.name: The Missing Number
levels.storyContext: Sir Calculate claims some numbers can NEVER appear in a skip-count...

problems.statement: "If you skip-count by 4 starting at 4 (4, 8, 12, 16...), will you ever land on 30? Prove your answer."

correctAnswer.value: No! Every number in the sequence is a multiple of 4, and 30 is not a multiple of 4 (30 ÷ 4 = 7 R2).
correctAnswer.displayValue: No — 30 is not a multiple of 4.

hints.text: What do all numbers in the sequence 4, 8, 12, 16, 20... have in common?
They are all multiples of 4. Is 30 a multiple of 4?
Check: 30 ÷ 4 = 7 remainder 2. Since the remainder is not 0, 30 is NOT a multiple of 4.

problems.solutionExplanation: No! Skip-counting by 4 only produces multiples of 4. Since 30 ÷ 4 = 7 R2 (remainder is not 0), 30 is not a multiple of 4 and will never appear.
problems.teachingPoint: Skip-counting by n only produces multiples of n — a number that is NOT a multiple can never appear in the sequence.

problems.statement: "Can two odd numbers add up to an odd number? Explain."

correctAnswer.displayValue: No — odd + odd is always even

hints.text: Every example gives an even sum. Can you explain why?
Odd = even + 1. So odd + odd = (even + 1) + (even + 1) = even + 2 = even.

problems.solutionExplanation: No — odd + odd always equals even. Example: (2k+1)+(2m+1) = 2(k+m+1), which is even.
problems.teachingPoint: Parity rule: odd + odd = even, even + even = even, odd + even = odd.

levels.name: Skip-Counting & Patterns Quiz
levels.storyContext: Show your pattern mastery!

problems.statement: "Count by 7s: 7, 14, 21, ___. What comes next?"

hints.text: Add 7 each time.

problems.teachingPoint: Skip-counting by 7: add 7 each step.

problems.statement: "Is 45 a multiple of both 5 and 9? A) Yes B) No"

hints.text: Check: is 45 ÷ 5 a whole number? Is 45 ÷ 9?
Both divide evenly, so yes.

problems.solutionExplanation: Yes — 45 = 5 × 9. It is a multiple of both.
problems.teachingPoint: A number that is a multiple of both a and b is a common multiple.

hints.text: Divide to find the missing factor.

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 — because 7 × 6 = 42.
problems.teachingPoint: Missing factor: divide the product by the known factor.

problems.statement: "What is the digit-sum rule for divisibility by 9?"

correctAnswer.value: A number is divisible by 9 if its digits add up to a multiple of 9.
correctAnswer.displayValue: Digits sum to a multiple of 9

hints.text: The digit sum equals 9 (or a multiple of 9) for all multiples of 9.
Rule: if digit sum is divisible by 9, the number is divisible by 9.

problems.solutionExplanation: If the sum of the digits is a multiple of 9, the number is divisible by 9.
problems.teachingPoint: Digit sum divisibility tests: works for both 3 and 9.

problems.statement: "Can three even numbers add up to 25? Explain."

correctAnswer.value: No. Even + even + even = even. 25 is odd.
correctAnswer.displayValue: No — sum of evens is always even

hints.text: Even + even = even. Then even + even = still even.
The sum of any number of even numbers is always even.
25 is odd. Three evens sum to an even number. So it is impossible.

problems.solutionExplanation: No — even + even + even is always even, but 25 is odd. Impossible.
problems.teachingPoint: Parity proof: sum of even numbers is always even.

chapters.name: Perimeter & Area Pass

levels.name: What is Perimeter?
levels.storyContext: What is Perimeter?

problems.statement: "You walk around a triangular meadow. The sides are 5 m, 7 m, and 8 m. How far did you walk in total?"

hints.text: If you walk ALL the way around the meadow, which edges do you walk along?
You walk along all 3 sides. Add up all the side lengths.

problems.solutionExplanation: 20 m — perimeter is the total distance around: 5 + 7 + 8 = 20 meters.
problems.teachingPoint: Perimeter = sum of all side lengths.

problems.statement: "A square has sides of 7 cm. What is its perimeter?"

hints.text: Perimeter is the distance around a shape. A square has 4 equal sides.
Perimeter = 4 × side length = 4 × 7.

problems.solutionExplanation: 28 cm — perimeter of a square = 4 × side = 4 × 7 = 28.
problems.teachingPoint: Square perimeter shortcut: P = 4 × s (since all 4 sides are equal).

problems.statement: "Which shape has a greater perimeter: a triangle with sides 8, 8, 8 or a square with sides 5? A) Triangle B) Square C) Same"

hints.text: Calculate each perimeter separately.
Triangle: 8+8+8 = 24. Square: 4×5 = 20.
24 > 20, so the triangle has a greater perimeter.

problems.solutionExplanation: Triangle — perimeter 24 (8+8+8) vs square perimeter 20 (4×5).
problems.teachingPoint: More sides does not always mean more perimeter — it depends on side lengths.

levels.name: Rectangle Perimeter
levels.storyContext: A rectangular cabin sits at the mountain pass.

problems.statement: "A rectangular cabin has length 10 ft and width 6 ft. What is its perimeter?"

hints.text: A rectangle has two pairs of equal sides. Which sides are equal?
Add all four sides: length + width + length + width.
That is 10 + 6 + 10 + 6. What is the total?

problems.solutionExplanation: 32 ft — perimeter = 10 + 6 + 10 + 6 = 32 feet.
problems.teachingPoint: Rectangle perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × width, because opposite sides are equal.

problems.statement: "A rectangle is 12 m long and 4 m wide. What is its perimeter?"

hints.text: Rectangle perimeter = 2 × (length + width).

problems.teachingPoint: Rectangle perimeter formula: P = 2 × (l + w) or P = 2l + 2w.

problems.statement: "A rectangle has perimeter 30 m and length 10 m. What is the width?"

hints.text: Use the perimeter formula: P = 2(l + w). Plug in what you know.

problems.teachingPoint: Working backwards with formulas: plug in known values and solve for the unknown.

levels.name: Isosceles Triangle Perimeter
levels.storyContext: An isosceles bridge spans a deep gorge.

problems.statement: "What is the perimeter of an isosceles triangle with sides of length 9 and 4?"

hints.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. But WHICH two are equal: the 9s or the 4s?
Could it be 4, 4, 9? Check: can two sides of length 4 reach across a gap of 9?
Triangle inequality: two sides must sum to MORE than the third. Does 4 + 4 > 9?

problems.solutionExplanation: 22 — only 9, 9, 4 forms a valid triangle (4+4=8 < 9 fails the triangle inequality), so perimeter = 9+9+4 = 22.
problems.teachingPoint: The triangle inequality (any two sides must sum to more than the third) eliminates impossible triangles — 4+4=8 < 9, so only 9+9+4 works.

problems.statement: "An isosceles triangle has two sides of 7 and a base of 10. What is its perimeter?"

hints.text: Isosceles triangles have two equal sides.
Add all three sides: 7 + 7 + 10.

problems.teachingPoint: Isosceles triangle: two sides equal, one different. P = 2×equal side + base.

problems.statement: "An equilateral triangle has perimeter 45 cm. What is the length of each side?"

hints.text: Equilateral = all 3 sides equal. P = 3 × side.
45 = 3 × side. So side = 45 ÷ 3.

problems.solutionExplanation: 15 cm — equilateral triangle: 45 ÷ 3 = 15.
problems.teachingPoint: Equilateral triangle perimeter: P = 3s, so s = P ÷ 3.

levels.name: Find the Missing Side
levels.storyContext: A mysterious square tile has markings around its edge.

problems.statement: "A square has perimeter 36 cm. What is the length of one side?"

hints.text: A square has 4 equal sides. If you know the total perimeter, how do you find one side?
Perimeter = 4 × side length. So side length = perimeter ÷ 4.
Calculate: 36 ÷ 4 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 9 cm — since a square has 4 equal sides, each side = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm.
problems.teachingPoint: Working backwards from perimeter: since all 4 sides of a square are equal, divide perimeter by 4 to find the side length.

problems.statement: "A rectangle has perimeter 40 cm and width 8 cm. What is the length?"

hints.text: P = 2(l + w). Plug in P = 40 and w = 8.

problems.teachingPoint: Finding a missing dimension: rearrange the perimeter formula to isolate the unknown.

problems.statement: "A regular pentagon has perimeter 35 cm. What is the length of each side?"

hints.text: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides.
P = 5 × side. So side = 35 ÷ 5.

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 cm — regular pentagon: 35 ÷ 5 = 7.
problems.teachingPoint: Regular polygon perimeter: P = n × s, where n = number of sides. So s = P ÷ n.

levels.name: What is Area?
levels.storyContext: The mountain meadow is divided into unit squares.

problems.statement: "Count the unit squares that cover this rectangle: [3 × 4 grid shown]. What is the area?"

hints.text: Area measures how much flat space a shape covers. How do you measure it?
Count each individual unit square inside the rectangle.
You can count row by row: how many squares in each row, times how many rows?

problems.solutionExplanation: 12 square units — the 3×4 grid has 3 rows of 4, so 3 × 4 = 12 unit squares.
problems.teachingPoint: Area counts the number of unit squares that cover a surface — for rectangles, this equals rows × columns.

problems.statement: "A rectangle is 5 units long and 3 units wide. What is its area in square units?"

hints.text: Area of a rectangle = length × width.
5 × 3 = 15 square units.

problems.solutionExplanation: 15 square units — area = 5 × 3 = 15.
problems.teachingPoint: Rectangle area: A = l × w. Each square unit is 1 unit × 1 unit.

problems.statement: "What unit measures area? A) cm B) cm² C) cm³ D) cm/s"

hints.text: Area measures how much surface a shape covers.
Perimeter uses cm (length). Area uses length × length = ?
cm × cm = cm². Area uses square units.

problems.solutionExplanation: cm² — area is measured in square units (cm², m², ft²).
problems.teachingPoint: Perimeter = linear units (cm, m). Area = square units (cm², m²). Volume = cubic units (cm³, m³).

levels.name: Rectangle Area
levels.storyContext: The cabin floor needs to be measured for new tiles.

problems.statement: "A cabin floor is 7 meters long and 5 meters wide. What is the area of the floor?"

hints.text: Area of a rectangle = length × width. What are the dimensions here?
Multiply the length (7) by the width (5).
Calculate: 7 × 5 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 35 square meters — area = length × width = 7 × 5 = 35 sq m.
problems.teachingPoint: Area of rectangle = length × width

problems.statement: "A square has sides of 9 m. What is its area?"

hints.text: Area of a square = side × side.

problems.solutionExplanation: 81 m² — area of a square = s² = 9² = 81.
problems.teachingPoint: Square area: A = s². This connects to perfect squares: 9² = 81.

problems.statement: "A rectangle has area 48 m² and length 8 m. What is the width?"

hints.text: Area = length × width. Plug in what you know.

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 m — from A = l × w: 48 = 8 × w, w = 6.
problems.teachingPoint: Finding missing dimensions from area: divide area by the known dimension.

levels.name: Area vs Perimeter
levels.storyContext: Two explorers debate whether perimeter or area matters more for their campsite.

problems.statement: "A rectangle is 6 units by 3 units. Calculate BOTH its perimeter AND its area."

hints.text: Perimeter and area use different formulas. Recall: perimeter adds sides, area multiplies.
Perimeter = 2×6 + 2×3. Area = 6 × 3. Calculate each.
Perimeter = 12 + 6 = 18. Area = 18. Notice anything surprising?

problems.solutionExplanation: Perimeter = 2(6+3) = 18 units. Area = 6×3 = 18 square units. Same number, different units!
problems.teachingPoint: Different measurements can have the same number but different units!

problems.statement: "A square has perimeter 20 cm. What is its area?"

hints.text: First find the side length from the perimeter.
P = 20, so side = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm.
Area = 5 × 5 = 25 cm².

problems.solutionExplanation: 25 cm² — side = 20 ÷ 4 = 5, area = 5² = 25.
problems.teachingPoint: Two-step problems: find the side from perimeter first, then compute area.

problems.statement: "Without calculating, which has more area: a 4×9 rectangle or a 6×6 square?"

hints.text: Calculate or estimate each area.
Both equal 36! Same area, different shapes.

problems.solutionExplanation: They are equal — both have area 36. Same area does not mean same shape.
problems.teachingPoint: Different rectangles can have the same area. A square maximizes area for a given perimeter.

levels.name: Complex Area
levels.storyContext: The great hall is divided into equal meeting rooms.

problems.statement: "A rectangle with width 21 ft and height 16 ft is split into six congruent rectangles arranged in a 2×3 pattern. What is the area of one small rectangle?"

hints.text: If you know the total area and the number of small rectangles, how do you find one?
First find the total area: 21 × 16. Then divide by 6.
Total area = 336 sq ft. Each small rectangle = 336 ÷ 6 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 56 sq ft — total area = 21 × 16 = 336, divided equally into 6 gives 336 ÷ 6 = 56.
problems.teachingPoint: Dividing area equally means dividing the total by the number of pieces — the arrangement does not change the math.

problems.statement: "An L-shaped room can be split into two rectangles: one is 4×3 and the other is 6×2. What is the total area?"

hints.text: To find the area of a complex shape, split it into simpler shapes.
Area of rectangle 1: 4 × 3 = 12. Area of rectangle 2: 6 × 2 = 12.
Total = 12 + 12 = 24 square units.

problems.solutionExplanation: 24 — split into two rectangles: 4×3 = 12 and 6×2 = 12. Total = 12 + 12 = 24.
problems.teachingPoint: Complex areas: decompose into rectangles, find each area, then add them together.

problems.statement: "A 10×8 rectangle has a 3×4 rectangle cut out of one corner. What is the remaining area?"

hints.text: Find the full area and subtract the cut-out.
Full area = 10 × 8 = 80. Cut-out = 3 × 4 = 12.
80 - 12 = 68 square units.

problems.solutionExplanation: 68 — full area 80 minus cutout 12 = 68.
problems.teachingPoint: Subtraction strategy: for shapes with pieces removed, find full area minus removed area.

levels.name: Area Puzzle
levels.storyContext: The architect must design the optimal campsite.

problems.statement: "A rectangle has a perimeter of 20 units. The length and width are whole numbers. What dimensions give the LARGEST possible area?"

hints.text: What whole-number pairs of length and width give a perimeter of 20?
If perimeter = 20, then length + width = 10. List all pairs: (1,9), (2,8), (3,7), (4,6), (5,5).
Calculate each area: 1×9=9, 2×8=16, 3×7=21, 4×6=24, 5×5=25. Which is largest?

problems.solutionExplanation: 5 × 5 = 25 square units. Among all rectangles with perimeter 20, the square maximizes area.
problems.teachingPoint: For a fixed perimeter, the shape closest to a square always has the largest area — this is a fundamental optimization principle.

problems.statement: "Two rectangles both have area 24 square units. One is 6×4. Find another rectangle with different dimensions but the same area."

hints.text: What pairs of whole numbers multiply to 24?
Any pair except 4×6 works: 3×8, 2×12, or 1×24.

problems.solutionExplanation: Multiple answers: 8×3, 12×2, or 24×1. All have area 24 but different dimensions.
problems.teachingPoint: Same area, different dimensions: finding all factor pairs reveals all possible rectangles.

problems.statement: "A rectangle has perimeter 20. List all whole-number length/width pairs and find which gives the MAXIMUM area."

hints.text: The maximum area is 25, from the 5×5 square.

problems.solutionExplanation: 25 — the square (5×5) gives maximum area. Pairs: 9, 16, 21, 24, 25. The more "square-like," the more area.
problems.teachingPoint: For a fixed perimeter, the square always gives the maximum area. This is a fundamental optimization principle.

levels.name: Grogg's Perimeter Blunder
levels.storyContext: Grogg measured the fence around a field, but his math is off...

problems.statement: "Grogg says a 5×8 rectangle has perimeter 26 because 5 + 8 + 5 + 8 = 26. Find his error."

correctAnswer.value: The perimeter is actually 26. Grogg is correct! 5+8+5+8 = 26.

hints.text: Check Grogg's addition carefully: 5 + 8 + 5 + 8.
Add step by step: 5+8=13, 13+5=18, 18+8=26. Is that right?
Actually, 5+8+5+8 = 26 IS correct. This is a trick question — sometimes Grogg gets it right!

problems.solutionExplanation: Grogg is actually correct! 5+8+5+8 = 26. The perimeter of a 5×8 rectangle is 26 units. Not every claim contains an error!
problems.teachingPoint: Critical thinking means checking EVERY claim, including ones that seem wrong — sometimes the work is correct and you must recognize that.

problems.statement: "Grogg says the area of a 7×3 rectangle is 20 because 7+3+7+3 = 20. What did he calculate instead?"

correctAnswer.value: Grogg calculated the perimeter (20), not the area. The area is 7 × 3 = 21.
correctAnswer.displayValue: He calculated perimeter, not area. Area = 21.

hints.text: Compare what Grogg did to the area formula.
Grogg added all sides: 7+3+7+3. That formula is for what measurement?
That is the perimeter formula! Area = length × width = 7 × 3 = 21.

problems.solutionExplanation: Grogg calculated the perimeter (7+3+7+3=20), not the area. Area = 7×3 = 21.
problems.teachingPoint: Common mistake: confusing perimeter (add all sides) with area (multiply length × width).

problems.statement: "Lizzie says a square with side 6 has perimeter 24 and area 24, so they are always equal. Find her error."

correctAnswer.value: It is a coincidence! A square with side 5 has P=20 but A=25. They are not always equal.
correctAnswer.displayValue: Coincidence — try side=5: P=20, A=25. Not always equal.

hints.text: Check if perimeter and area are always equal for squares.
Try a different side length. Side = 5: P = 20, A = 25. Are they equal?
No! P=20 ≠ A=25. Side 6 is special but it is a coincidence, not a rule.

problems.solutionExplanation: Coincidence! For side 5: P=20 but A=25. For side 3: P=12 but A=9. Perimeter and area are NOT always equal.
problems.teachingPoint: Perimeter and area use different operations (addition vs multiplication) and different units (cm vs cm²). Equality is coincidental.

levels.name: The Odd Perimeter Question
levels.storyContext: Sir Calculate poses a deep question about rectangles...

problems.statement: "Can a rectangle with whole-number sides have an odd perimeter? Prove your answer."

correctAnswer.value: No! Perimeter = 2(L+W) is always even because multiplying by 2 always gives an even number.

hints.text: What is the formula for the perimeter of a rectangle?
Perimeter = 2 × (length + width). What happens when you multiply ANY number by 2?
Multiplying by 2 always gives an even result. So 2 × (anything) = even. Can it ever be odd?

problems.solutionExplanation: No! Perimeter = 2(L+W). Since 2 times any whole number is even, the perimeter is always even. An odd perimeter is impossible.
problems.teachingPoint: Impossibility proofs use structure — here, the factor of 2 in the perimeter formula guarantees an even result, no matter what L and W are.

problems.statement: "Can a rectangle have perimeter 15 with whole-number sides? Prove your answer."

correctAnswer.value: No. Perimeter = 2(l+w), so P is always even for whole-number sides. 15 is odd.
correctAnswer.displayValue: No — P = 2(l+w) is always even, but 15 is odd.

hints.text: Rectangle perimeter = 2(l + w). What do you notice about the factor of 2?
If l and w are whole numbers, then l+w is a whole number, and 2×(whole number) is always...
Always even! 2 × anything = even. So perimeter 15 (odd) is impossible.

problems.solutionExplanation: No — rectangle perimeter = 2(l+w) is always even when sides are whole numbers. 15 is odd, so impossible.
problems.teachingPoint: The factor of 2 in P = 2(l+w) guarantees even perimeter. This is an impossibility proof by parity.

levels.name: Perimeter & Area Quiz
levels.storyContext: Show your mastery of perimeter and area!

problems.statement: "A rectangle is 9 m long and 4 m wide. What is its perimeter?"

hints.text: Perimeter = 2 × (length + width).

problems.teachingPoint: Rectangle perimeter: P = 2(l + w).

problems.statement: "What is the area of a rectangle that is 11 m by 7 m?"

hints.text: Area = length × width.

problems.teachingPoint: Rectangle area: A = l × w.

problems.statement: "A square has area 64 cm². What is the length of one side?"

hints.text: Area of a square = side². What number squared gives 64?
8² = 64, so side = 8 cm.

problems.solutionExplanation: 8 cm — because 8² = 64.
problems.teachingPoint: Finding side from area: take the square root. 64 = 8².

problems.statement: "A rectangle has perimeter 28 and area 48. What are its length and width?"

hints.text: You need two numbers where l+w = 14 (from P=28) and l×w = 48.
Try factor pairs of 48: 1×48, 2×24, 3×16, 4×12, 6×8. Which sums to 14?

problems.solutionExplanation: 8 × 6 — they sum to 14 (perimeter/2) and multiply to 48 (area).
problems.teachingPoint: Finding dimensions from P and A: you need two numbers that sum to P/2 and multiply to A.

problems.statement: "Two rectangles: 3×12 and 6×6. Without computing, which has more perimeter and which has more area?"

value: 6×6 has more area (36 vs 36)... actually equal area!

hints.text: Think about how stretching a rectangle affects P and A.
More elongated = more perimeter. Same area here (36 each).

problems.solutionExplanation: 3×12 has more perimeter (30 vs 24). Both have area 36. Elongated shapes have more perimeter for the same area.
problems.teachingPoint: Key insight: for the same area, elongated rectangles have MORE perimeter. Squares have the LEAST perimeter.

signatureContent: Area as covering with unit squares

levels.name: What is Multiplication?
levels.storyContext: Base camp has rows of tents, each holding climbers.

problems.statement: "There are 4 tents at base camp. Each tent has 3 climbers. How many climbers in total? Write this as both addition and multiplication."

hints.text: You have 4 groups of 3. How would you add 3 four times?
Write it as addition first: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = ?
Now write the same thing as multiplication: how many groups × how many in each group?

problems.solutionExplanation: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, or 4 × 3 = 12. Multiplication is a shortcut for repeated addition.
problems.teachingPoint: Multiplication is a shortcut for repeated addition.

levels.name: The Commutative Property
levels.storyContext: Two explorers arrange the same supplies in different patterns.

problems.solutionExplanation: Yes, both equal 24. A 6×4 array rotated 90° becomes a 4×6 array — the commutative property says order does not matter.

problems.statement: "Lizzie says 5 × 8 = 40 but 8 × 5 must be different because 8 is first now. Is she right?"

levels.name: Using Commutativity
levels.storyContext: Lizzie shows a faster way to count the trail markers.

problems.statement: "What is 5 × 60?"

problems.teachingPoint: Use known benchmarks to estimate: 7 × 3 = 21 < 25, 7 × 4 = 28 > 25.

levels.name: The Associative Property
levels.storyContext: Three teams of climbers can be grouped different ways.

problems.statement: "Calculate (2 × 3) × 4 and 2 × (3 × 4). What do you notice?"

hints.text: Calculate each expression step by step. Do you get the same answer?
Both equal 24. This works for ANY three numbers — that is the associative property.

problems.solutionExplanation: Both equal 24. (2×3)×4 = 6×4 = 24 and 2×(3×4) = 2×12 = 24. Grouping does not change the product.
problems.teachingPoint: (a × b) × c = a × (b × c) (The Associative Property)

problems.statement: "Calculate (5 × 2) × 3. Enter the result."

hints.text: Follow the order of operations: parentheses first.
10 × 3 = 30. The associative property says you get the same answer grouping differently.

problems.teachingPoint: The associative property lets you group factors however you like — the product stays the same.

problems.statement: "Which grouping makes 4 × 5 × 2 easiest to compute? A) (4 × 5) × 2 B) 4 × (5 × 2) C) (4 × 2) × 5"

hints.text: Which pair of numbers creates a "friendly" number when multiplied?
5 × 2 = 10 — that is a very friendly number! What does multiplying by 10 give?
4 × (5 × 2) = 4 × 10 = 40. Creating a 10 makes it the simplest calculation.

problems.solutionExplanation: B is easiest: 4 × (5 × 2) = 4 × 10 = 40. Pairing 5 and 2 creates 10.
problems.teachingPoint: Look for pairs that make 10 or 100 — these are the friendliest groupings.

levels.name: Strategic Grouping
levels.storyContext: The supply master groups items for the easiest count.

problems.statement: "Calculate 5 × 7 × 2 by grouping the easy numbers first."

hints.text: Look for two numbers that multiply to give a "friendly" number like 10.
Which two of 5, 7, 2 multiply to make 10?

problems.solutionExplanation: 70 — group 5 × 2 first to get 10, then 10 × 7 = 70. Strategic grouping makes it easy!
problems.teachingPoint: Strategic grouping (associative property) lets you create friendly numbers like 10 or 100 to simplify multiplication.

problems.statement: "Calculate 2 × 8 × 5 using strategic grouping."

hints.text: Look for two numbers that pair nicely.
2 × 5 = 10. Can you use that?

problems.teachingPoint: Always look for a factor pair that makes 10: 2 × 5 = 10 is the most common friendly pair.

problems.statement: "What is 4 × 25?"

hints.text: 4 × 25 is a famous friendly product. Can you see why?
Think: 25 is a quarter of 100. How many quarters make a whole?
4 quarters = 1 whole. So 4 × 25 = 100.

problems.solutionExplanation: 100 — four quarters make one dollar! 4 × 25 = 100.
problems.teachingPoint: 4 × 25 = 100 is a key benchmark fact. Memorize friendly products like this.

problems.statement: "Without calculating exactly, which is greater: 7 × 40 or 6 × 50?"

hints.text: Both involve multiplying by multiples of 10. Can you use basic facts?
7 × 40 = 280 and 6 × 50 = 300. Which is larger?

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 × 50 = 300 > 7 × 40 = 280. Breaking into basic fact × 10 makes comparison easy.
problems.teachingPoint: To compare products with multiples of 10, reduce to basic facts first: 7×4=28 vs 6×5=30.

levels.name: Multiplication Puzzles
levels.storyContext: Ancient puzzles guard the multiplication temple.

problems.statement: "Fill in the blanks: ___ × ___ = 36, where both numbers are greater than 1 and less than 10. Find ALL solutions."

hints.text: Think about which pairs of numbers from 2-9 multiply to give 36.
Start with small factors: does 2 × ? = 36? Does 3 × ? = 36? Continue...
Check: 4 × 9 = 36 ✓. Is there a perfect square? 6 × 6 = 36 ✓. Don't forget reverse order.

problems.solutionExplanation: 4 × 9, 6 × 6, and 9 × 4. These are all factor pairs of 36 with both numbers between 2 and 9.
problems.teachingPoint: Finding all factor pairs systematically means checking each number from 2 upward — stop when factors start repeating.

problems.statement: "Find two single-digit numbers (both > 1) that multiply to 48. List all pairs."

hints.text: Try each number from 2 through 9 as a factor of 48.
Does 2 work? 48 ÷ 2 = 24 (too big). Does 3? 48 ÷ 3 = 16 (too big). Keep going...
48 ÷ 6 = 8 ✓. Both 6 and 8 are single digits. Is there another pair?

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 × 8 = 48 (and 8 × 6). No other pair of single-digit numbers > 1 works.
problems.teachingPoint: Systematic factor search: try each divisor from 2 upward until the factors start repeating.

problems.statement: "If □ × 7 = 63, what is □?"

hints.text: This is a missing-factor problem. What operation undoes multiplication?
Divide both sides by 7: □ = 63 ÷ 7.

problems.solutionExplanation: 9 — because 63 ÷ 7 = 9, and we can verify: 9 × 7 = 63.
problems.teachingPoint: Missing-factor problems use division: if □ × b = c, then □ = c ÷ b.

levels.name: Three-Number Products
levels.storyContext: Three treasure chests each contain treasure to count.

problems.statement: "What is 5 × 4 × 5?"

hints.text: Look for a strategic grouping that makes this easier.
Can you pair two of the numbers to make a friendly product?

problems.statement: "What is 2 × 3 × 15?"

Try grouping 2 × 15 first: 2 × 15 = 30. Then 30 × 3 = ?

problems.teachingPoint: Multiple grouping strategies work — pick the one that creates the friendliest intermediate result.

Way 1: (2 × 5) × 9. Way 2: 2 × (5 × 9). Calculate each.

levels.name: Grogg's Multiplication Mistake
levels.storyContext: Grogg proudly shows his work, but something is wrong...

problems.statement: "Grogg says: 6 × 7 = 43 because 6 × 7 = 6 × 6 + 7 = 36 + 7 = 43. Find his mistake and give the correct answer."

hints.text: Grogg tried to break 6 × 7 into 6 × 6 + something. Is that valid?

problems.solutionExplanation: Grogg incorrectly added 7 instead of 6. By the distributive property: 6×7 = 6×(6+1) = 36+6 = 42.
problems.teachingPoint: When breaking apart multiplication, BOTH factors matter: 6 × 7 = 6 × 6 + 6 × 1, NOT 6 × 6 + 7.

problems.statement: "Grogg says 8 × 5 = 8 × 4 + 5 = 32 + 5 = 37. Find his error and give the correct answer."

correctAnswer.value: 8 × 5 = 40, not 37. Grogg should have added 8, not 5: 8×4 + 8×1 = 32 + 8 = 40.

hints.text: Grogg tried to break 8 × 5 into 8 × 4 + something. What should the "something" be?
8 × 5 = 8 × (4 + 1) = 8 × 4 + 8 × 1. Grogg wrote + 5 instead of + ?
The correct breakdown: 8 × 4 + 8 = 32 + 8 = 40, not 32 + 5 = 37.

problems.solutionExplanation: Grogg wrote +5 instead of +8. Correct: 8×5 = 8×(4+1) = 8×4 + 8×1 = 32 + 8 = 40.
problems.teachingPoint: When using the distributive property, BOTH parts get multiplied: a × (b+c) = a×b + a×c, not a×b + c.

problems.statement: "What is 6 × 80?"

hints.text: This is a basic fact times a multiple of 10.

levels.name: Quick Comparison

problems.statement: "Is 5 × 90 more or less than 500?"

problems.teachingPoint: The associative property: (a × b) × c = a × (b × c). Parentheses can move freely in multiplication.

problems.statement: "Order from least to greatest: 8 × 6, 7 × 7, 9 × 5"

levels.name: Why Odd Numbers Make Squares
levels.storyContext: Professor Owlbert reveals the deep reason behind the odd number pattern...

problems.statement: "A 3×3 square has 9 dots. To make it a 4×4 square, you add an L-shaped border. How many dots are in the L-shaped border? Why is this always an odd number?"

correctAnswer.value: 7 dots in the L-border (4+4-1=7). It is odd because you add one row (4) + one column (4) minus the shared corner (1) = 2n-1, which is always odd.

hints.text: Draw a 3×3 square. Now extend it to 4×4. What new dots did you add?
You add a new bottom row (4 dots) and a new right column (4 dots), but the corner is shared.
New dots = 4 + 4 - 1 = 7. In general, going from n×n to (n+1)×(n+1) adds 2(n+1) - 1 dots.

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 dots in the L-border. You add a row of 4 + column of 4, minus 1 shared corner = 7. Formula: 2n+1 where n is the new side length minus 1.
problems.teachingPoint: The visual L-border proof shows WHY consecutive square differences are odd: adding a row + column - shared corner always gives an odd number.

problems.statement: "The first 4 odd numbers are 1,3,5,7. Their sum is 16 = 4². Use this pattern to predict the sum of the first 10 odd numbers."

hints.text: The pattern: sum of first n odds = n².

problems.solutionExplanation: 100 — sum of first 10 odd numbers = 10² = 100. The pattern holds for all n.
problems.teachingPoint: Mathematical patterns let us predict without computing: sum of n odds = n² is a powerful shortcut.

Odd × odd = odd because (2k+1)(2k+1) = 4k²+4k+1 = even+1 = odd.

problems.solutionExplanation: Yes — odd × odd = odd. The square of an odd number is always odd.
problems.teachingPoint: Parity preservation: odd×odd=odd, even×even=even. Squaring preserves parity.

levels.name: Order of Operations Introduction

The rule says: multiplication before addition. So compute 4 × 2 first.

Correct: (2+5) = 7, then 7 × 3 = 21.

problems.solutionExplanation: Grogg ignored the parentheses. Correct: (2+5)×3 = 7×3 = 21, not 17.
problems.teachingPoint: Parentheses are NOT optional — they change the order of computation.

levels.name: Practice Order of Operations

levels.name: Area Model Introduction
levels.storyContext: The area model map shows how to break apart multiplications.

problems.statement: "To find 7 × 12, break 12 into 10 + 2. Draw an area model and solve."

hints.text: Breaking a number into parts can make multiplication easier. How would you split 12?
Break 12 into 10 + 2. Then multiply each part by 7 separately.
Draw a rectangle: 7 tall, split into 10 wide and 2 wide. Each part is 7×10 and 7×2.

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 × 12 = 7 × (10+2) = 70 + 14 = 84. The area model shows this as two rectangles that together make the whole.
problems.teachingPoint: The area model visualizes why the distributive property works — splitting a rectangle into parts does not change its total area.

problems.teachingPoint: The area model splits one factor: a×(b+c) = a×b + a×c. This IS the distributive property.

problems.teachingPoint: The distributive property: a×(b+c) = a×b + a×c. Both parts get multiplied by a.

levels.name: The Distributive Property
levels.storyContext: "The ancient Distributive Property lets you 'distribute' multiplication across addition!"

problems.statement: "Use the distributive property to calculate 6 × 15 by breaking 15 into 10 + 5."

Break 15 into 10 + 5. Then multiply 6 by each part.

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 × 15 = 6 × (10+5) = 60 + 30 = 90. The distributive property splits a hard multiplication into two easy ones.

levels.name: Breaking Apart Factors

problems.statement: "Calculate 8 × 99 using the distributive property."

problems.solutionExplanation: 8 × 99 = 8 × (100-1) = 800 - 8 = 792. Breaking 99 into 100-1 makes the calculation easy.
problems.teachingPoint: The distributive property works with subtraction too: a × (b - c) = ab - ac. Using nearby friendly numbers like 100 is a powerful shortcut.

levels.name: Why Distribution Works
levels.storyContext: Professor Owlbert asks the deep question: WHY does the distributive property work?

problems.statement: "Using an area model, explain WHY 4 × (3 + 5) must equal 4 × 3 + 4 × 5. What makes this true, not just a trick?"

correctAnswer.value: A 4×8 rectangle can be split into a 4×3 and a 4×5 rectangle. The total area does not change — just how you partition it.
correctAnswer.displayValue: Splitting a rectangle does not change its total area.

hints.text: Draw a rectangle that is 4 units tall and (3+5)=8 units wide.
Now draw a vertical line splitting it into a 4×3 part and a 4×5 part. Did any area disappear?
The total area is the same whether you measure it as one rectangle (4×8) or two parts (4×3 + 4×5).

problems.solutionExplanation: A 4×8 rectangle has area 32. Splitting it into 4×3 (12) and 4×5 (20) gives 12+20 = 32. Splitting does not change total area — that IS the distributive property.
problems.teachingPoint: The distributive property is not a "trick" — it is a geometric fact: splitting a rectangle into parts does not change its total area.

problems.statement: "Does distribution work with subtraction? Is 5×(8-3) = 5×8 - 5×3? A) Yes B) No"

problems.teachingPoint: The distributive property works over subtraction too: a×(b-c) = a×b - a×c.

hints.text: Division means sharing equally. How would you split 24 into 4 equal groups?
Think: what number times 4 gives 24?
Try: 4 × 6 = 24. So each group has how many?

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 — dividing 24 hikers into 4 equal groups gives 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hikers per group.
problems.teachingPoint: Division answers "How many in each group?" or "How many groups?"

problems.statement: "20 cookies shared equally among 4 friends. How many does each get?"

hints.text: Division means sharing equally.
20 ÷ 4 = 5 cookies each.

problems.solutionExplanation: 5 — 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cookies per friend.
problems.teachingPoint: Division is sharing equally: total ÷ groups = items per group.

problems.statement: "18 ÷ 3 can also be read as: A) 18 groups of 3 B) How many 3s make 18 C) 18 minus 3 D) 3 times 18"

hints.text: Division asks: how many groups of the divisor fit in the dividend?
18 ÷ 3 asks: how many groups of 3 are in 18?

problems.solutionExplanation: B — 18 ÷ 3 asks "how many 3s make 18?" Answer: 6 groups.
problems.teachingPoint: Division is the inverse of multiplication: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 because 6 × 3 = 18.

levels.name: Division as Reverse Multiplication
levels.storyContext: The multiplication-division connection is carved on the wall.

hints.text: Division and multiplication are inverse operations — they undo each other.
If 7 × 8 = 56, then 56 ÷ 8 must give back one of the original numbers.
56 ÷ 8 = ? (which factor is missing?)

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 — since 7 × 8 = 56, dividing 56 by 8 gives back 7. Division undoes multiplication.
problems.teachingPoint: Division undoes multiplication. If a × b = c, then c ÷ b = a.

hints.text: Division reverses multiplication.
If 7 × 9 = 63, then 63 ÷ 9 = the other factor.

problems.teachingPoint: Every multiplication fact gives two division facts: if a × b = c, then c ÷ a = b and c ÷ b = a.

problems.statement: "Which multiplication fact helps solve 56 ÷ 8? A) 7×7=49 B) 7×8=56 C) 8×8=64 D) 6×8=48"

hints.text: Find which fact has 56 as the product.
Look for ___ × 8 = 56.

problems.solutionExplanation: B — 7 × 8 = 56, so 56 ÷ 8 = 7. Use multiplication facts to solve division.
problems.teachingPoint: Think multiplication to solve division: find what times the divisor equals the dividend.

levels.name: Division Facts
levels.storyContext: Quick division facts unlock the next passage.

hints.text: Think: what number times 9 gives 63?
Try the 9 times table: 9×5=45, 9×6=54, 9×7=?

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 — from the multiplication fact 9 × 7 = 63, we get 63 ÷ 9 = 7.
problems.teachingPoint: Division facts are just multiplication facts read backwards — knowing one gives you the other for free.

hints.text: What × 8 = 72?

problems.solutionExplanation: 9 — because 8 × 9 = 72.
problems.teachingPoint: Division fact families: 72 ÷ 8 = 9, 72 ÷ 9 = 8, 8 × 9 = 72.

hints.text: What × 5 = 45?

problems.solutionExplanation: 9 — because 5 × 9 = 45.
problems.teachingPoint: Dividing by 5: double the number then divide by 10 (or use multiplication facts).

hints.text: What × 12 = 108? Try building up: 12×9 = ?

problems.teachingPoint: For larger divisors, use estimation or break apart: 12×10=120, so 12×9=120-12=108.

levels.name: Division with Arrays
levels.storyContext: Dots on the cave ceiling form a perfect array.

problems.statement: "45 dots are arranged in 5 equal rows. How many dots in each row? Write this as a division."

hints.text: An array with 45 dots in 5 equal rows — how many per row?
This is a division problem: 45 ÷ 5 = ?
Think: 5 × ? = 45. Try 5 × 9.

problems.solutionExplanation: 9 dots per row. 45 ÷ 5 = 9. The array shows 5 rows of 9.
problems.teachingPoint: Arrays connect multiplication and division visually — the same array shows both 5 × 9 = 45 and 45 ÷ 5 = 9.

problems.statement: "A 4 × 6 array has 24 objects. If you divide into rows of 4, how many rows?"

hints.text: Division from an array: total ÷ items per row = rows.

problems.teachingPoint: Arrays show division visually: total ÷ row size = number of rows.

problems.statement: "Put these division facts in order from smallest to largest quotient: 36÷4, 36÷6, 36÷9, 36÷12"

hints.text: Calculate each quotient.

problems.solutionExplanation: 36÷12=3, 36÷9=4, 36÷6=6, 36÷4=9. Larger divisor = smaller quotient.
problems.teachingPoint: When dividing the same number, a larger divisor gives a smaller quotient.

levels.name: What are Remainders?
levels.storyContext: Not everyone fits into a group — some are left over.

problems.statement: "14 hikers want to form groups of 3. How many complete groups? How many hikers are left over?"

hints.text: When you cannot divide evenly, there is a remainder — the "left over" amount.
How many complete groups of 3 can you make from 14?
Try: 3 × 4 = 12 (fits), 3 × 5 = 15 (too big). So 4 groups with 14 - 12 = ? left over.

problems.solutionExplanation: 4 groups with 2 left over (14 ÷ 3 = 4 R2). The remainder is what cannot fill another complete group.
problems.teachingPoint: The leftover is called the "remainder." We write 14 ÷ 3 = 4 R2.

problems.statement: "17 ÷ 5 = ___ remainder ___. Fill in both blanks."

hints.text: How many times does 5 fit into 17?
5×3=15, 5×4=20 (too big). So 3 times with some left.
17 - 15 = 2 left over. Answer: 3 R 2.

problems.solutionExplanation: 3 R 2 — 5 × 3 = 15, and 17 - 15 = 2 remainder.
problems.teachingPoint: Remainder = dividend - (divisor × quotient). The remainder must be less than the divisor.

problems.statement: "What is the remainder when 29 is divided by 6?"

hints.text: Find the largest multiple of 6 that is ≤ 29.
6×4=24, 6×5=30 (too big). So quotient=4.
29 - 24 = 5. The remainder is 5.

problems.teachingPoint: Finding remainders: find the closest multiple below, then subtract.

levels.name: Finding Remainders
levels.storyContext: The remainder reveals which path to take.

problems.statement: "What is 23 ÷ 5?"

hints.text: Find the largest multiple of 5 that does not exceed 23.
5 × 4 = 20, 5 × 5 = 25 (too big). So the quotient is 4.
The remainder is 23 - 20 = ?

problems.teachingPoint: To find a remainder: find the largest multiple of the divisor that fits, then subtract it from the dividend.

problems.statement: "23 students need to sit in rows of 4. How many full rows? How many students in the last row?"

correctAnswer.value: 5 full rows, 3 in the last row

hints.text: Divide 23 by 4 to find rows and remainder.
23 ÷ 4 = 5 R 3. Five full rows of 4 = 20. Three remain.
5 rows × 4 = 20 students seated. 23 - 20 = 3 in the last row.

problems.solutionExplanation: 5 full rows with 3 in the last row. 23 = 5×4 + 3.
problems.teachingPoint: Real-world remainders: the leftover students still need a row, even if it is not full.

problems.statement: "What is the remainder when 100 is divided by 7?"

hints.text: Find the largest multiple of 7 that is ≤ 100.
100 - 98 = 2. Remainder = 2.

problems.teachingPoint: For larger numbers, estimate: 7×10=70, 7×14=98, 7×15=105>100. So quotient=14, remainder=2.

levels.name: Remainder Patterns
levels.storyContext: A pattern in remainders unlocks the cipher.

problems.statement: "When dividing by 6, what are all the possible remainders?"

hints.text: When dividing by 6, the remainder is what is "left over" after grouping by 6.
Can the remainder ever be 6 or more? Think about what would happen.
If the remainder were 6, you could make another group! So remainders must be less than the divisor.

problems.solutionExplanation: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — the remainder when dividing by 6 is always less than 6.
problems.teachingPoint: The remainder is always less than the divisor — if it were equal or larger, you could make another complete group.

problems.statement: "When you divide any number by 5, what are the possible remainders? A) 0-4 B) 0-5 C) 1-4 D) 1-5"

hints.text: The remainder must be less than the divisor.
When dividing by 5, the remainder can be 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4.
Remainder = 5 is not possible because that would mean another full group of 5.

problems.solutionExplanation: A — remainders when dividing by 5 are 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4. Never 5 or more.
problems.teachingPoint: When dividing by n, remainders range from 0 to n-1. A remainder of n means one more full group.

problems.statement: "What remainders are possible when dividing by 3? List all of them."

hints.text: The remainder must be less than the divisor (3).
Possible remainders: 0, 1, 2. Never 3 (that would be a full group).
0, 1, 2 — three possible remainders when dividing by 3.

problems.solutionExplanation: 0, 1, 2 — when dividing by 3, remainder ∈ {0, 1, 2}.
problems.teachingPoint: Dividing by n gives n possible remainders: 0, 1, 2, ..., n-1.

levels.name: Remainder Word Problem
levels.storyContext: The baker at base camp needs help boxing cookies.

problems.statement: "A baker has 50 cookies. She puts 8 cookies in each box. How many full boxes can she make? How many cookies are left over?"

hints.text: How many times does 8 fit into 50 without going over?
Try: 8 × 6 = 48 (fits), 8 × 7 = 56 (too big).
So 6 full boxes. The leftovers: 50 - 48 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 full boxes with 2 cookies left over. 50 ÷ 8 = 6 R2 (8×6=48, 50-48=2).
problems.teachingPoint: In real-world division, the remainder matters: you can only count COMPLETE boxes, and the remainder tells you what is left.

problems.statement: "A farmer packs eggs in boxes of 12. He has 50 eggs. How many full boxes? How many eggs left over?"

hints.text: Divide 50 by 12.
12×4=48, 12×5=60 (too many). So 4 full boxes.
50 - 48 = 2 eggs left over.

problems.solutionExplanation: 4 full boxes (with 2 eggs left). 50 ÷ 12 = 4 R 2.
problems.teachingPoint: Real-world division: the quotient tells you full groups, the remainder is what is left.

problems.statement: "38 people need taxis. Each taxi holds 4. How many taxis are needed?"

correctAnswer.displayValue: 10 (round up because 2 people need a ride)

hints.text: 38 ÷ 4 = ? with remainder. But here you must round UP.
38 ÷ 4 = 9 R 2. But the 2 remaining people still need a taxi!
9 + 1 = 10 taxis needed. When people cannot be left behind, round up.

problems.solutionExplanation: 10 taxis — 38 ÷ 4 = 9 R 2, but the 2 extra people need a taxi too. Always round UP for "how many needed" problems.
problems.teachingPoint: Context matters with remainders: sometimes round down (full boxes), sometimes round up (taxis needed).

levels.name: Chicken McNugget Problem
levels.storyContext: An ancient weight puzzle with special constraints.

problems.statement: "Fubert has only 3-gram and 7-gram weights. What is the largest weight that he CANNOT make by combining two or more of these weights?"

hints.text: List the weights you CAN make using only 3-gram and 7-gram weights.
You can make: 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16... Which ones are MISSING?
Cannot make: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 11. What is the largest number in this list?

problems.teachingPoint: This is a Frobenius/coin problem — for two coprime values a and b, the largest impossible value is ab - a - b.

problems.statement: "Can you buy exactly 20 chicken nuggets using only boxes of 6 and boxes of 9?"

correctAnswer.value: No. 6a + 9b = 20 has no solution with non-negative integers.
correctAnswer.displayValue: No — no combination of 6s and 9s makes 20

hints.text: Try all combinations of 6 and 9.
0 nines: 6a=20, not possible. 1 nine: 6a=11, not possible. 2 nines: 6a=2, not possible.
